paragraphs: Ilai the elder, Rabbi Yehudah’s father, a tanna and Rabbi Eliezer’s student, Pasin, mishnah 6, 23a. The Mishnah has Rabbi Ilai say, “I heard from Rabbi Elazar” (it should be Eliezer, as in the passage there 26a), “and went around all his students to see whether they heard it from him, but found no fellow.” Tosafot 26, beginning of b: Pesachim 39a teaches, “Until I came to Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov, who agreed with me.” Though Rabbi Eliezer ben Yaakov was Rabbi Akiva’s student, Rabbi Ilai lived long. Sukkah 27b: he went to greet his teacher Rabbi Eliezer in Lod on the festival. Rabbi Eliezer told him, “Ilai, you are not among those resting for the festival,” for Rabbi Eliezer used to say, “I praise the idle who do not leave their homes on the festival.” Do not be misled into thinking he went to greet Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua on the festival, and Rabbi Elazar ben Shammua told him, “For Rabbi Eliezer says, I praise the idle”—meaning Rabbi Eliezer the great, son of Hyrcanus. This is not so, since Rabbi Eliezer the great was Rabbi Ilai’s teacher. Rather, the anonymous Gemara and its arranger brought “Rabbi Eliezer used to say,” meaning Rabbi Eliezer the great regularly said, “I praise the idle.” Likewise everywhere “he used to say” means he regularly said it. Avot, chapter 1, similarly, “He used to say,” etc., because he regularly said so. That is, Rabbi Eliezer’s “You are not among those resting for the festival” is as though he said, “Do I not regularly say, I praise,” etc.? Hakometz Hamminchah 18a: Rabbi Yehudah was Rabbi Ilai’s son, and Rabbi Ilai was Rabbi Eliezer’s student. He is called elder in Chagigah 16a; Mo'ed Katan 17; Kiddushin 40a. Rabbi Ilai the elder said, “If you see the evil inclination overpowering you, go to a place where you are unknown.” He followed Rabban Gamliel of Yavneh. Rabban Gamliel found a loaf and told him, “Ilai, take it,” etc.; see there. He presented before Rabbi Eliezer and Rabbi Yehoshua, Pesachim 38b. He asked Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Eliezer, and presented the matters before Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah, Tosefta, Challah, chapter 1.

Yuchasin writes, in the chronological section under Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Ilai: “Rabbi Ilai was Rabbi Yishmael’s colleague.” (In the tannaim’s order, in his own entry, Yuchasin writes “like a colleague.”) “Gittin, chapter 1: someone came before Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Ilai. I find it difficult: how could Rabbi Ilai, father of Rabbi Yehudah, Rabbi’s teacher, bring an objection from the Mishnah Rabbi made from Rabbi Meir’s statement, when Rabbi Meir was later than Rabbi Yishmael? Moreover, Rabbi Meir was Rabbi Yishmael’s student. It also seems Rabbi Yishmael was greater than Rabbi Ilai, since the latter called him ‘my teacher,’ and Rabbi Yishmael called him ‘my son.’ Afterward I found this incident in Tosefta Gittin, where Rabbi Ilai does not mention Rabbi Meir; this pleased me.” End quotation. The Tosefta’s wording: “An incident: someone from Kefar Sisi brought Rabbi Yishmael a woman’s bill of divorce. He told him, ‘You too must say, It was written before me and signed before me’; he did not require witnesses. After the man left, Rabbi Ilai said before him, ‘My teacher, Kefar Sisi is within the Land of Israel’s boundary, closer to Sepphoris than Akko.’ He replied, ‘Since the matter came out permissibly, let it stand.’” End quotation. To explain the matter, I bring the Gemara, Gittin 6, beginning of b: “A man brought a bill of divorce before Rabbi Yishmael. He asked, ‘Must I say it was written before me and signed before me?’ He replied, ‘My son, whence are you?’ ‘From Kefar Sisai.’ ‘You must say it was written and signed before me, so you will not need witnesses.’ After he left, Rabbi Ilai entered: ‘My teacher, is not Kefar Sisai,’ etc., ‘and we learned, Rabbi Meir says,’ etc.? He replied, ‘Be silent, my son,’ etc.” The Gemara asks: Rabbi Yishmael said “so you will not need witnesses” (not because it was necessary; what difficulty did Rabbi Ilai see?). It answers: they did not finish reporting Rabbi Yishmael’s statement to Rabbi Ilai. I do not understand his words: “I find it difficult how Rabbi Ilai objected from the Mishnah Rabbi made from Rabbi Meir’s statement, Meir being later than Yishmael, and Yehudah son of Ilai being Rabbi’s teacher.” What is Rabbi doing here? Who mentioned him? Were Rabbi Meir’s sayings unknown before Rabbi arranged the Mishnah? If his question is how one objects to Rabbi Yishmael from Rabbi Meir, his student, why add, “Moreover, Rabbi Meir was Rabbi Yishmael’s student”? He also wanted to prove Rabbi Ilai was Rabbi Yishmael’s colleague from “a man came before Rabbi Yishmael and Rabbi Ilai”: since the man came before both and asked them, they must be equals and colleagues. On the contrary, he asked Rabbi Yishmael whether he must say “written before me and signed before me”; after that man left, Rabbi Ilai entered, as above. Rabbi Ilai called Rabbi Yishmael “my teacher,” and Rabbi Yishmael called him “my son,” suggesting Rabbi Yishmael was his teacher, as he himself wrote. As for objecting from Rabbi Meir the student to Rabbi Yishmael his teacher, he overlooked what I wrote in the rules: the Talmud sometimes objects from a student to his teacher, since presumably the student heard his statement from his teacher. Thus the answer is sound: Rabbi Yishmael too agrees with Rabbi Meir that it is unnecessary, except to avoid needing witnesses, and they had not finished reporting it before him. Why then did the Tosefta please him for omitting Rabbi Ilai’s mention of Rabbi Meir? General practice follows these three elders: Rabbi Ilai concerning the first fleece, Rabbi Yoshiyah, and Rabbi Yehudah ben Beteira, Berakhot 22a; Jerusalem Talmud there, mishnah 4; Chullin 137b. Emek Hammelekh 75b: Joseph’s trial with Potiphar’s wife came to Rabbi Ilai, and this was a reincarnation of Rabbi Yehudah son of Rabbi Ilai. Rabbi Yochanan son of Rabbi Ilai—perhaps his son.
